Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative relies primarily on vivid, real-time scenes—the three crossings with different passengers (Peters, the cyclist, and Frau Mewes) and the final solitary crossing when the phone rings—which make the story engaging and reveal Ilse's stoic character through dialogue and physical action. At the same time, the writer skillfully weaves in brief passages of exposition and summary to explain how the hand-pulled ferry operates, provide context about the regular passengers, and compress the quiet waiting periods between crossings (such as the twenty-minute wait at the Dömitz shore). This balance maintains a rhythmic, unhurried pace that mirrors the movement of the river and the ferry itself.
